name: AI Company Operations
guide:
AI Company Operations roles handle the business machinery behind an AI company rather than the AI product itself. In our sample of 36 postings this covers finance leadership such as strategic finance leads and finance managers, legal and compliance counsel focused on AI products, technical and executive recruiters who staff AI research and engineering teams, and general operations managers who run data operations, revenue operations, or enterprise AI delivery. This is different from AI Product Management or Program Management, which own the roadmap for an AI feature or coordinate a cross functional launch. Operations roles instead keep the company running, covering payroll, hiring pipelines, contracts, and the internal processes that let product and research teams function. Readers often mix these up because both titles carry the word AI, but the daily work rarely overlaps.

Our postings rarely spell out a required degree, though the legal counsel roles at OpenAI, Notion, Abridge, and Vanguard assume a law degree and bar admission, since these are product counsel and general counsel positions. Finance roles at Databricks and Perplexity lean toward a background in accounting or finance, though the postings in our sample do not name a specific degree requirement. We did not find any postings in this category naming a professional certification such as SHRM, CPA, or PMP, so we will not claim one is expected here. The honest read from our data is that most operations postings screen on relevant company stage experience rather than a credential checklist.

Seniority in our sample runs from junior counsel roles up through manager, lead, principal, and one executive level opening. The middle of the market is the busiest tier, with mid-level titles like recruiter, product counsel, and finance specialist making up the largest single group in our postings. Manager level titles, covering operations managers and finance managers, form the next largest cluster, and these typically expect several years running a function rather than just participating in one. What tends to get someone hired at the senior end is prior experience inside a fast growing AI or software company specifically, since postings for counsel and recruiter roles from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Together AI read as wanting familiarity with how AI companies actually hire, contract, and ship product.

Named tools and frameworks that recur in our skills data include AWS for cloud infrastructure, Okta for identity and access management, and Databricks, Python, and SQL for the finance and data operations postings. Compliance and governance terms appear often too, including NIST, HIPAA, and GDPR, reflecting how much of AI company operations work now touches regulatory risk. A working familiarity with large language models shows up across recruiter and counsel postings alike, even when the role itself is not technical, because hiring and advising for AI teams requires understanding what those teams build. We did not see software engineering skills required outside of the data and finance postings, so most people in this category should not expect to write code day to day.

As of today we currently track approximately 18 open postings in AI Company Operations, drawn from a broader sample of 36 postings we pulled for this guide. Only 3 of those 36 postings listed a salary figure, at Chenega MIOS, Ensemble Health Partners, and Vanguard, ranging from $120,274 to $145,018 per year, so we cannot state a reliable market wide salary range from our data. The companies posting most often in this category are OpenAI and Bjak with 5 postings each, followed by Databricks and Voize with 3 each, and Waymo and Abridge with 2 each. This is a thin sample relative to engineering or product roles at these same companies, and it tells its own story, since AI company operations hiring tends to move in smaller batches than technical hiring. We will keep tracking this category and update these numbers as more postings come in.

reading.body:
AI companies are hiring heavily for legal, finance, and talent acquisition roles rather than AI research and engineering positions, signaling that operational scaling now constrains growth more than research capability.

The 18 openings split sharply between roles managing risk and resources—counsel for product and AI governance, finance specialists, operations managers—and talent acquisition itself. OpenAI alone has three active recruiter roles across geographies. This pattern reflects a mature constraint. Early-stage AI companies faced bottlenecks in research output and compute access. These postings suggest the constraint has shifted upstream: companies can acquire compute and build products, but cannot manage the legal exposure, financial complexity, and talent scarcity without dedicated infrastructure.

The concentration of legal hires is notable. Four of the 18 positions are counsel roles focused on AI product, data, and digital assets. This reflects genuine new risk—liability frameworks around AI systems remain unsettled, and companies selling or deploying AI face regulatory uncertainty that engineering alone cannot solve. Finance and operations hires cluster at Databricks and among newer entrants like Perplexity and Abridge, not only at incumbents.

The data does not capture how many positions go unfilled, whether these roles are new or replacements, or how compensation compares to research positions. It shows intent to hire, not hiring velocity or success. Geographic distribution spans San Francisco, London, Bengaluru, and the UAE, but the dataset size is too small to map where AI operations capacity is concentrating.
